title: North Korea’s Enemies Within
gist: Drawing on a decade of interviews with elite defectors, Jieun Baek argues that North Korean elite loyalty to Kim Jong Un is increasingly performative and driven by self-preservation, as purges, surveillance, lack of security, and marketization erode genuine conviction. The regime is not near collapse because atomization prevents collective action, but a succession struggle or economic shock could trigger mass elite defection or withdrawal of cooperation.

insights.claim: As of August 2024, South Korea's National Intelligence Service reported that elite defections under Kim Jong Un were two and a half times the combined total under Kim Il Sung and Kim Jong Il.
insights.speaker: Jieun Baek
insights.so_what: Signals rising internal strain in North Korea, though not imminent collapse.
insights.quote: the number of defections from North Korea’s upper class recorded under Kim Jong Un was two and a half times the combined total observed during the reigns of Kim Il Sung (1948 to 1994) and Kim Jong Il (1994 to 2011)
insights.locator: Those North Koreans who still manage

insights.claim: The absolute number of elite defections remains small, in the hundreds, and Baek warns against reading the trend as a harbinger of imminent regime collapse.
insights.speaker: Jieun Baek
insights.so_what: Korean peninsula regime-change scenarios remain low probability in the near term.
insights.locator: Those North Koreans who still manage

insights.claim: Since Kim sealed borders during COVID-19, the number of North Korean defectors reaching South Korea has plummeted, and the borders remain sealed with information more controlled than ever.
insights.speaker: Jieun Baek
insights.so_what: North Korea is more closed post-pandemic, reducing visibility into regime stability.
insights.locator: Since Kim Jong Un came to power

insights.claim: Most of the more than 34,000 North Koreans in South Korea came from poor northern border provinces, unlike elite escapees from Pyongyang, a city of roughly three million in a country of 25 million.
insights.speaker: Jieun Baek
insights.so_what: Elite defectors are a distinct and more strategically informative group.
insights.locator: Most of the more than 34,000

insights.claim: No escapee is known to have come from the central ranks of the Organization and Guidance Department, the party's most powerful agency.
insights.speaker: Jieun Baek
insights.so_what: The regime's core control apparatus remains intact.
insights.quote: No escapee is known to have come from the OGD’s central ranks
insights.locator: The Organization and Guidance Department

themes.theme: Mechanics of control and preference falsification

insights.claim: North Korea's regime does not need every official to believe in it; it needs doubters to feel isolated in their skepticism.
insights.speaker: Jieun Baek
insights.so_what: Regime durability rests on atomization; watch for signs of elite coordination as a key risk indicator.
insights.quote: The regime does not need every official to believe in it. But it needs its doubters to feel isolated and alone in their skepticism and disillusionment.
insights.locator: Those North Koreans who still manage

insights.claim: North Korea is not truly a 'Hermit Kingdom': it is nuclear-armed, has diplomatic relations with over 160 countries, the world's fourth-largest standing army and highly skilled cyber-operators.
insights.speaker: Jieun Baek
insights.so_what: North Korea's cyber and military capabilities make it a persistent global risk actor.
insights.locator: North Korea has long been referred

insights.claim: Diplomats and workers abroad must surrender passports, leave relatives as collateral, and undergo month-long ideological reviews on return.
insights.speaker: Jieun Baek
insights.so_what: Illustrates control intensity that suppresses defection and information flow.
insights.locator: The Organization and Guidance Department

insights.claim: Preference falsification is endemic in Pyongyang: elites coordinate self-criticism sessions in advance and stage public grief, so belief and cynicism coexist in the same office and person.
insights.speaker: Jieun Baek
insights.so_what: Outward loyalty signals are unreliable indicators of regime stability.
insights.locator: Scholars refer to this gap

insights.claim: Pyongyang treats prominent defections as security emergencies because they show others with private doubts that they are not alone; after a 2016 group restaurant defection in China, all other workers in China were recalled for interrogation.
insights.speaker: Jieun Baek
insights.so_what: Elite defections can cascade, which is why the regime reacts aggressively.
insights.locator: When elites do leave, their departures

insights.claim: Jang Song Thaek's 2013 execution signaled to all elites that no one, even a member of the ruling family, was untouchable, and prompted defections such as Ri Jong Ho's family in 2014.
insights.speaker: Jieun Baek
insights.so_what: Purges raise elite insecurity, increasing long-run defection risk.
insights.locator: The shocking 2013 execution

insights.claim: In some border cities such as Sinuiju, the party has recently banned any unapproved gatherings of three or more people.
insights.speaker: Jieun Baek
insights.so_what: Shows tightening social controls, a sign of regime anxiety.
insights.locator: Most people opt to stay.

insights.claim: Elites have strong incentives to stay because defection means losing status and purpose, as illustrated by a former official reduced to warehouse work in South Korea.
insights.speaker: Jieun Baek
insights.so_what: Explains why the privilege-plus-coercion bargain still holds.
insights.locator: The prospect of losing that status

insights.claim: The elite bargain has an expiration date: retired senior officers and cadres receive no pensions and lose state-provided cars, homes and appliances, often becoming guards or market vendors.
insights.speaker: Jieun Baek
insights.so_what: Younger elites accumulate private wealth, accelerating marketization.
insights.quote: Yet this bargain has an expiration date.
insights.locator: Yet this bargain has an expiration date.

insights.claim: Younger elite families increasingly prefer business, technical work, study abroad and private wealth over long army conscription or party careers, and would welcome economic liberalization.
insights.speaker: Jieun Baek
insights.so_what: Latent demand for economic opening could matter if regime policy shifts.
insights.locator: Younger and middle-aged elites

insights.claim: Money is reshaping North Korea's order: titles are valued for conversion into income, marriage prospects favor access to foreign currency, and state-regulated markets have hosted over 10,000 vendors.
insights.speaker: Jieun Baek
insights.so_what: De facto marketization is entrenched despite official socialism.
insights.locator: Money has altered the old order

insights.claim: Kim has accommodated markets by regulating and taxing them, allowing a controlled intranet and smartphones, and letting officials do business if they pay mandatory 'loyalty funds'.
insights.speaker: Jieun Baek
insights.so_what: The state extracts rents from markets, a funding source for the regime.
insights.locator: Kim has accommodated some of these

insights.claim: What Kim cannot offer elites is dependable, lasting safety, since everything remains subordinate to the leader's whims and patrons can be purged.
insights.speaker: Jieun Baek
insights.so_what: The core grievance is structural and cannot be fixed without weakening Kim's control.
insights.locator: What Kim cannot offer is dependable

insights.claim: The regime is funded by trade with China, weapons sales, cybertheft from foreign banks and companies, and laborers sent abroad, which pay for nuclear weapons, security services, prison camps and elite luxuries.
insights.speaker: Jieun Baek
insights.so_what: North Korean cybertheft targeting banks and companies is a funding pillar and ongoing security risk.
insights.locator: The regime has other sources of durability.

insights.claim: A disaffected elite has five options: silence, flight, parallel networks, protest, or incremental reform; the last three are extraordinarily dangerous, so most stay silent or defect.
insights.speaker: Jieun Baek
insights.so_what: Useful framework for assessing regime-change pathways.
insights.locator: Growing elite grievances do not mean

insights.claim: The most plausible organized threat to the Kim regime would be elite-driven from Pyongyang rather than a mass revolt from below.
insights.speaker: Jieun Baek
insights.so_what: Monitor elite purges and succession signals rather than popular unrest.
insights.quote: a challenge or rebellion is more likely to start among elite insiders than as a mass revolt from below
insights.locator: This helps explain another surprising

insights.claim: To win elite confidence Kim would have to end purges, collective punishment and prison camps and allow freer information and markets, but each concession would embolden elites against him, so he will likely not relax his grip.
insights.speaker: Jieun Baek
insights.so_what: No liberalization expected; North Korea policy stays rigid.
insights.locator: Kim Jong Un can continue to manage

insights.claim: The accumulated costs of performative loyalty will become most dangerous during a succession struggle or severe economic shock, such as a coup, a Mount Paektu eruption or an economic meltdown, when officials may withhold cooperation or defect en masse.
insights.speaker: Jieun Baek
insights.so_what: Tail-risk scenario for Korean peninsula instability tied to succession or shocks.
insights.locator: He will likely not relax

insights.claim: A North Korean interpreter who entered South Korea's embassy in Ulaanbaatar in August 2025 seeking to defect remains in limbo a year later, as Mongolia has been slow to cooperate and Seoul's left-leaning government won't confirm the case.
insights.speaker: Jieun Baek
insights.so_what: Seoul's engagement-oriented government is downplaying defections to warm ties with Pyongyang.
insights.locator: In August 2025, a North Korean

insights.claim: Elite North Korean defectors seeking U.S. asylum have had claims languish for years or be rejected, with one waiting over nine years, which may signal to wavering elites that staying put is safer.
insights.speaker: Jieun Baek
insights.so_what: U.S. asylum policy reduces incentives for elite defection, indirectly bolstering regime stability.
insights.locator: Several elite defectors I spoke with

insights.claim: Kim will face his last days when enough elites conclude that remaining loyal is no longer their safest and most rational choice.
insights.speaker: Jieun Baek
insights.so_what: Regime fall would be sudden and elite-driven, hard to forecast from outside.
insights.quote: Kim will face his last days when a large enough body of North Korean elites conclude that remaining loyal is no longer their safest and most rational choice.
